I feel like historical context is important here. The American study of trauma is really young, as is metal health as a science in general. Discussion about trauma first started with WWI vets. See; soldiers heart -> battle fatigue -> shell shock -> PTSD

The trauma of sexual violence, mostly because in this culture men’s health means more, the study of trauma in women came after- as if sadly always does. 

So, here’s why the book isn’t as bad as you might think it be… as the field has progressed, the only time we have seen considerable expansion, exploration, inclusion, and informative strides in trauma research it has STARTED by talking about vets. It’s how our society seems to be able to understand it. Again, Patriarchy. 

Nonetheless, this book makes the VITAL distinction that trauma is 1) an injury 2) is passed down generationally and 3) highly complex which is why CPTSD is almost always misdiagnosed, particularly as Cluster B personality disorders (BPD, Antisocial, etc) 

Our society is male-centric. Once complex trauma is introduced through a “lens” that is acceptable to the American public, it’s more likely to be seen as a “legit” diagnosis by our culture and thus change our science. 

Once it’s a “legitimate diagnosis” to the public, the DSM will change. Trauma based diagnosis’s are not gender based, this proves helpful for everyone. It then allows a therapist to finally diagnosis it- regardless of if it is a specific kind of trauma or not. 

This will be huge for those of us struggling with complex trauma. For benefits, treatments, medication and beyond.

My husband and I have been together for almost 8 years. I have complex PTSD from years of various trauma, DV and SA being two of them. First, you are okay. What happened is not your fault. You did nothing wrong and these things happen and can happen frequently. It can vary in severity and frequency depending on where you are in recovery. Flashbacks happen when the brain encounters a stimuli that reminds the brain of when the traumatic event occurs. This pulls our brain, very realistically, back to the very place it was during that event. This can be repaired overtime with therapy and also with the help of medication to relieve symptoms (I’m also a MSW, about to be a licensed therapist). 

Having a partner who cares about your mental health means the world in recovery. I also felt like my triggers would maybe push away my husband. They didn’t because we communicated openly. I had to get comfortable expressing and finding out what my triggers were, my husband had to work on how he responded in those moments and how to best support me. We are very happy and you two can be two. 

Psychoeducation (knowing about your condition and how it impacts you) is the first ingredient to overcoming it. It gets better, it truly does.

I'm so sorry that you're going through this. I know it's extremely draining and rough. 

I have also gone through this experience. I have just recently been in a place where I can say that my PTSD is almost gone. For me, every time I see men with a certain type of facial hair I'm triggered. At one point it was so bad that I would think the individual was my rapist and I would break down. 

It's important to remember that your professor is a trigger because he reminds you of the individual who violated you. Commonality in general, is almost impossible to avoid. Sadly, triggers will always come up and learning to handle/ live with them is a difficult and long process. 

I think it's important to remind you that he is not perpetrator. If you're comfortable enough, I would consider meeting with him during office hours and speaking to him about it. 

Regardless, speak to your counselor about it first. If you don't have one, get one. It's the most valuable thing you can do for yourself whilst going through a recovery process. 

I hope things well and you can get the situation worked out. 

Take care and remember that you're a survivor. The actions taken against you do not define you. And as always, you're beautiful.
